title: The whole body
hook: steps three and four: sensing the whole body, calming it

segments.voice: Yesterday, long and short: steps one and two, knowing the breath as it is. Your line was just know it. In a tense moment, was your breath long or short? Day one hundred and nine.

Right now, without moving, notice your shoulders. Are they up near your ears? Now your jaw. Is it clenched? Your forehead. Your hands. Most people find at least one spot holding on for no reason at all. We carry our bodies around all day like a bag we've forgotten we're holding. Steps three and four of the breathing discourse bring the body back into the picture. First, feel all of it. Then, let it settle.
screen: `SHOULDERS UP NEAR YOUR EARS?` → `A BAG YOU FORGOT YOU'RE HOLDING.` → `FEEL ALL OF IT. LET IT SETTLE.`

segments.voice: Notice a small shift in the words here. Steps one and two said: a person knows. Steps three and four say: a person trains. They train like this: experiencing the whole body, I will breathe in; experiencing the whole body, I will breathe out. Then: calming the body's activity, I will breathe in; calming it, I will breathe out. Knowing has become training. Something is being gently developed now. But what does the whole body mean? Here's where Buddhists read the text differently, and it's worth knowing both. The Visuddhimagga, the old manual, says the body here is the body of the breath: you feel each breath from its beginning, through its middle, to its end, the whole length of it, not just the tip. Many modern teachers read it as the physical body: you let the breath be felt everywhere, chest, belly, back, shoulders, the whole body breathing. Both readings are practiced today, and both lead somewhere good. And then step four: calming. The word for the body's activity, in a related discourse, is explained as the breath itself. So as you feel the whole body, the breath naturally softens and slows, and the body goes quiet with it. You don't force it. You create the conditions, and the settling happens, like mud sinking to the bottom of a still glass of water. This is where many people first notice why the Buddha called breathing a pleasant way to dwell. The shoulders come down. The jaw lets go. The body settles.
screen: `FROM KNOWING TO TRAINING.` · `THE WHOLE BREATH, OR THE WHOLE BODY?` · `CALMING THE BODY'S ACTIVITY.` · `MUD SINKING IN STILL WATER.` · then, large: `THE BODY SETTLES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and find the breath. Now widen your attention, so you feel each breath from its very beginning to its very end. Then widen further: feel the breath moving the belly, the chest, the back, the shoulders. The whole body breathing. As you breathe out, let one place soften: the jaw, then the shoulders, then the hands. Don't force the calm. Just let the body find its own stillness, breath by breath. The bell holds the time.
The whole body. Steps three and four: feeling the whole breath, or the whole body, and letting it calm.
Your line: the body settles. Today, three times, feel one whole breath through your body, and let your shoulders drop. Day one hundred and nine.

howItsDone: In Buddhist breath meditation, practitioners move from simply knowing the breath to feeling it through its whole length, or through the whole body, and letting the body grow calm.

fork.setup: you're told to feel the whole body while breathing. which reading does the old manual give?
options: the whole breath, beginning, middle and end.
only the tip of the nose.
fork.reveal: the Visuddhimagga reads it as the whole body of the breath. many modern teachers read it as the physical body, and both are practiced.

original.note: Pali: body, and also a group or collection; which body is meant here is debated.

trapdoor: what you thought: relax your whole body.
what it means: feeling the breath fully, and letting the body's activity calm by itself.
what a scholar hears: kaya can mean a collection, which lets the Visuddhimagga read 'the whole breath-body'; MN 44 explains the bodily formation (kayasankhara) as in-and-out breathing.

notes: The two readings of 'whole body' (breath-body per the Visuddhimagga; physical body per many modern teachers) are presented without ranking; confirm.
The mud-in-water image is the writer's illustration, not from the text.
'A pleasant way to dwell': SN 54.9/54.11 call concentration by mindfulness of breathing a pleasant dwelling; paraphrased.
